https://enrsi.stvr.sk/articles/news/4554.text: Slovak Television and Radio is opening a special exhibition to celebrate 100 years of radio broadcasting and 70 years of television broadcasting in Slovakia. The exhibition opens to the public on August 3rd at the Slovak Radio building in Bratislava and will run until November 3rd. Divided into three sections, it presents the history of Slovak radio and television, displays historic broadcasting equipment and features well-known children's characters. Visitors can also use an audio guide available in ten languages, including Romani and Rusyn. The recordings were produced by journalists from minority-language editorial teams and Radio Slovakia International without the use of artificial intelligence. According to Slovak Radio Director Peter Janků, the exhibition offers visitors an opportunity to reflect on a century of broadcasting history in the iconic inverted pyramid building. Source: STVR

https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/c4gd24.text: Watch: Moment 64-year-old Nepali woman is found alive in mud-buried home Watch: Moment 64-year-old Nepali woman is found alive in mud-buried home Close More than 10 days after a wall of ice, rock and mud tore through a Himalayan valley in Nepal, rescuers continue to find survivors. Chandika Shrestha, a 64-year-old woman, was discovered alive on the fourth floor of her partially buried house in the Nuwakot district by Nepal's Armed Police Force on 5 September, according to Reuters. She was airlifted to a hospital in Kathmandu for treatment, Reuters reported. More on this story. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Light plane plunges into Queensland paddock, sparks grass fire A light aircraft has plunged into a rural property in Queensland, sparking a fast‑moving grass fire and a massive emergency response, with grave fears held for the people on board, AAP reports. The plane went down on a paddock south of Brisbane after 11am on Monday, with shocked residents raising the alarm as smoke billowed across paddocks. Crews were called to a grass fire just after 11am and arrived to find plane debris scattered on the Chambers Flat property and flames racing through dry grass across an area about 300 by 400 metres, authorities said. At least a dozen fire trucks and multiple crews worked to contain the blaze, which burned close to a farmhouse before being brought under control about 12.50pm. No homes were damaged. Police have cordoned off the crash site and have yet to confirm how many people were on board or whether anyone has been injured. Paramedics and firefighters remain at the scene as investigator

https://www.theguardian.com/news/audio/2.text: 00:00:00 00:00:00 Today in Focus Russia The Pussy Riot activist turned Kremlin informer – podcast Their opposition to Putin led to two of the group being sent to brutal prison camps. Then another was found to be spying for the Kremlin. Shaun Walker reports More ways to listen Apple podcasts Spotify RSS Feed Download Presented by Helen Pidd with Shaun Walker ; produced by Ivor Manley and Rudi Zygadlo ; executive producer Homa Khaleeli Mon 28 Sep 2026 22.00 EDT Share It’s January 2012 and Pussy Riot are filming a video in Red Square, Moscow. As snow covers the cobbles and dusts the onion globes of St Basil’s Cathedral, the clock on the Kremlin chimes 11am. Eight women in colourful balaclavas leap on to a stone platform, one with an electric guitar. They start playing their latest song, Putin Has Chickened Out. It’s pretty punchy, with lyrics such as: “The rebellious column is heading to the Kremlin / Windows are exploding in FSB offices.” The group had formed a few months earlier after Vladimir Putin announced that he planned to return to the Kremlin for a third term as president. Inspired by the Arab spring the previous year, they hoped to bring revolution to Russia and stop Putin. Instead, the state cracked down hard. Three Pussy Riot members were found guilty of hooliganism after later protests, with two spending two years in some of Russia’s harshest jails. Then, in August this year, another video featuring a Pussy Riot member, Rita Flores, went viral. This time, it wasn’t a punk performance. Flores had a confession. She was an informant for the FSB, the Russian intelligence service, she said. She told the Guardian’s special correspondent Shaun Walker her story. About how her handlers threatened and cajoled her into spying on the other artists in her collective and how she tried to thwart them. Meanwhile, Helen Pidd calls Masha Alekhina , a founder member of Pussy Riot who was jailed for her support of the group and fled the country. Alekhina tells Helen about why she does not feel angry at her former comrade in activism.
